strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: principled online RL training of discrete diffusion policies for combinatorial action spaces, filling a gap relative to the well-studied continuous-diffusion-RL literature.

The core methodological idea—casting the PMD policy-improvement step as a distributional-matching problem and deriving tractable forward-KL (ELBO-weighted self-imitation) and reverse-KL (via ELBO-difference or single-step augmented-MDP importance ratios) objectives—is theoretically motivated, with derivations and proofs provided in the appendix.

Broad and diverse experimental validation across three qualitatively different domains: single-step reward fine-tuning (DNA sequences), long-horizon macro-action RL (MinAtar/Atari), and cooperative multi-agent RL (Google Research Football), demonstrating the generality of the framework.

Useful practical contributions beyond the core algorithm: on-policy diffusion training to align training/inference distributions, a principled temperature auto-tuning scheme via Lagrangian duality, and inference-time sampling techniques (top-p, remasking) that improve efficiency for long macro-actions.
Reasonably thorough ablations (architecture, on-policy training, temperature tuning, sampling technique, scalability vs. macro-action length) that support the design choices.
Reports efficiency gains over the DRAKES baseline (substantially lower GPU memory and wall-clock time) which strengthens the practical significance claim.
weaknesses: Several headline results show implausibly large improvement factors (e.g., RL-D2 achieving 178.9K±64.6K vs. ~1.1K for the best baseline on Space Invaders, or 20.18K±3.75K vs. ~300 on Breakout in Table 1), which is at minimum under-explained and raises concerns about experimental fairness, potential differences in effective action-space definitions, or measurement artifacts; the paper does not investigate or justify why gains of this magnitude occur.

The comparison between the macro-action diffusion policy and single-step baselines (DQN, IMPALA, PPO, R2D2) in Fig. 2/Table 5 conflates the benefit of macro-action commitment itself with the benefit of the diffusion parameterization; while DQN-Macro/IMPALA-Macro control for macro-actions to some degree, the gap between RL-D2 and these macro baselines is still enormous and not sufficiently analyzed (e.g., no controlled study isolating representation power from action horizon effects).

Reported variances are very large in many settings with only 3 random seeds, which is a thin basis for statistical confidence on high-variance Atari benchmarks, and no significance testing is reported.

Reverse KL divergence relies on two approximate importance-sampling ratio estimators (biased ELBO-difference and single-step augmented-MDP ratio) whose bias/variance tradeoffs are not empirically compared or quantified, despite this being central to the RKL variant used in the MARL experiments.

No overall convergence or sample-complexity guarantee is given for the proposed algorithm despite building on PMD theory that provides such guarantees in the tabular/regularized setting; the theoretical contribution is limited to KL-bound derivations rather than end-to-end guarantees for the diffusion-parameterized policy.

Presentation has multiple rough edges: a broken/incomplete citation and sentence ("()zekri2025fine", the abrupt cutoff "We only need to change" in Appendix C.3), garbled/duplicated bibliography entries, and generally dense notation that could benefit from a cleaner main-text summary of the algorithm (e.g., pseudocode for the main training loop is missing from the main paper, only appearing implicitly).

No mention of code/data release or artifact availability, which limits reproducibility given the many implementation-specific choices (network architectures, hyperparameters, importance-ratio estimator selection per domain) documented only in extensive appendices.

Baselines for the Atari/MinAtar macro-action experiments are relatively dated (DQN, IMPALA, PPO, R2D2); no comparison to more recent or stronger sequence-model-based macro-action policies (e.g., autoregressive transformer policies, as used for the football experiments) is included in the Atari section, weakening the case that expressiveness specifically from diffusion (rather than any expressive sequence model) is responsible for gains.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and previously unexplored gap: principled online RL training of discrete diffusion policies for combinatorial action spaces, via a clean theoretical connection to policy mirror descent (target distribution derived analytically, then approximated via FKL/RKL distributional matching).
Both FKL and RKL update rules are derived with formal proofs (Appendix B) connecting them back to the PMD objective, giving the method a principled foundation rather than being purely heuristic.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation across three qualitatively different combinatorial domains: single-step DNA sequence generation (bandit), long-horizon Atari with macro-actions, and cooperative multi-agent joint-action learning in Google Research Football — this breadth is unusual and strengthens claims of generality.

Careful baseline design: naive exponential-output (DQN-Macro) and factored (IMPALA-Macro) adaptations, autoregressive joint-action baselines, and strong domain SOTA (DRAKES, MAT, MAPPO) directly test the paper's core hypotheses about combinatorial scaling and causal-order bias.

Rich ablation studies (temperature auto-tuning via KL-constrained duality, on-policy diffusion training, sampling strategies such as top-p and remasking, network architecture, planning with diffusion) that substantively probe design choices rather than just reporting headline numbers.

Good methodological rigor in statistical reporting (stratified bootstrap CIs over 168 Atari runs) and honest discussion of a real FKL/RKL trade-off (sample efficiency vs. asymptotic stability), including reporting failure modes (e.g., FKL collapse under poor temperature tuning, RKL failure in the low-sample GRF regime).
Demonstrated practical efficiency gains over a strong reward fine-tuning baseline (DRAKES) in GPU memory and wall-clock time for the DNA task.
weaknesses: The FKL loss relies on a self-normalized importance-weighted approximation of the softmax reweighting over a small sampled action subset (Appendix B.1); no bias/variance analysis is provided for this approximation in truly large combinatorial spaces, despite this being central to the method's tractability.

The RKL importance ratio uses a single-step augmented-MDP approximation (borrowed from Ren et al. 2024) whose approximation quality/bias relative to the true sequence-level likelihood ratio is not analyzed, only justified empirically.

Mixed/underwhelming results in places undercut the 'state-of-the-art' framing: in MinAtar (Table 1) RL-D2 is not best in 3 of 5 games (Asterix, Seaquest), and RKL fails outright (0.0 win rate) in the low-budget 11v11 GRF ablation—these are honestly reported but somewhat at odds with strong claims in the abstract/intro.

No theoretical convergence or sample-complexity guarantees are given for the practical FKL/RKL algorithms; the PMD convergence theory cited is for the idealized target, not the diffusion-approximated policy update actually used.

Limited comparison to other expressive policy parameterizations for combinatorial actions (e.g., factored/structured generative models, other non-causal generative classes) beyond autoregressive transformers, making it harder to isolate whether gains stem specifically from the diffusion parameterization versus the PMD-based training scheme itself.
Hyperparameter search for baselines is fairly limited (only shown for DQN-Macro), raising some concern about whether other baselines (IMPALA-Macro, MAT, MAPPO) were tuned as thoroughly as RL-D2.

The broader impact/ethics statement is minimal and generic, offering no substantive discussion despite the method's applicability to real-world systems like recommendation and multi-agent coordination.

No explicit mention of code release, which combined with the complexity of the training pipeline (distributed RL infrastructure, custom augmented-MDP ratios, temperature tuning) raises reproducibility concerns despite detailed hyperparameter tables.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and reasonably novel framework (RL-D2) that connects policy mirror descent theory with discrete diffusion model training, turning the RL policy-improvement step into a tractable distributional-matching problem via forward/reverse KL objectives.

Extensive and diverse experimental validation across three genuinely different combinatorial-action domains (DNA sequence generation, Atari with macro-actions, and cooperative MARL in Google Research Football), which strengthens claims of general applicability.

Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance versus multiple relevant baselines (DRAKES, DQN/IMPALA-Macro, MAT/MAPPO, autoregressive samplers), including favorable computational efficiency comparisons (e.g., large GPU memory/time reduction versus DRAKES).

Thoughtful ablation studies covering FKL vs. RKL trade-offs, temperature auto-tuning via hard KL constraints, on-policy diffusion training, sampling techniques (top-p, remasking), scalability with macro-action length, and network architecture choices.
Careful statistical reporting using stratified bootstrap confidence intervals across many seeds/tasks, and fairly detailed hyperparameter/appendix documentation that aids reproducibility.
Derivations for the FKL and RKL losses are provided with proofs in the appendix, giving the method some theoretical grounding beyond pure heuristics.
weaknesses: The forward-KL objective is only a tractable upper bound (via the diffusion ELBO and subsampled action sets), so the strong empirical FKL results lack the same theoretical improvement guarantees claimed for RKL; the practical algorithm deviates non-trivially from the idealized PMD target, and this gap is not deeply analyzed.

The RKL importance-sampling ratio construction (augmented MDP over diffusion steps, single-step ratio) is adapted directly from prior work (Ren et al., 2024) on continuous diffusion policies, somewhat limiting the originality of this component.

Some result framing is optimistic: e.g., in MinAtar (Table 1) RL-D2 only wins in 2 of 5 games and is clearly outperformed by DQN in Asterix and by DQN-Macro in Seaquest, yet the narrative emphasizes RL-D2's superiority; likewise in Atari, RL-D2 loses on roughly 20/56 games, which is understated in the main text relative to the state-of-the-art framing.

Baseline tuning appears asymmetric — a hyperparameter search is performed for DQN-Macro but not explicitly for IMPALA-Macro or other adapted baselines, raising some concern about fairness of comparisons.

No substantive discussion of limitations or failure modes in the main text (e.g., when diffusion policies underperform, sensitivity to temperature/KL-constraint schedules causing collapse as shown in the appendix, or scaling limits of the fixed-length sequence assumption for genuinely variable-size combinatorial actions); the Impact Statement is a boilerplate placeholder with no engagement with limitations or ethical considerations.

The method has many interacting design choices (PMD target, FKL/RKL choice, temperature schedule, on-policy diffusion training, sampling technique) each requiring careful tuning, which may hinder practical reproducibility and adoption despite the appendix ablations.

Comparisons are largely against classical or autoregressive baselines; there is limited comparison against other recent discrete-diffusion-policy or discrete generative RL methods beyond DRAKES, leaving open how RL-D2 compares to a broader landscape of emerging discrete diffusion RL approaches.
